channel.title: FDE Field Notes
channel.description: Field notes on deployment-engineering practice — discovery, scoping, customer judgment calls, and the skill nobody puts in the job posting.

item.title: Refusal as Engineering Gate
item.description: The three diagnostic moments where an FDE's highest-leverage act is saying 'don't build this yet'—before premature engineering locks in failure.

item.title: Context Is the Integration
item.description: MCP turned FDE glue code into a durable asset the customer owns. The work that's left — and that now matters most — is curating what each connector puts in front of the model.

item.title: The Harness Moves the Number
item.description: Same 4B model, same task, a 60-to-82% accuracy swing from harness design alone. The eval harness is the FDE's real deliverable — and the acceptance contract with the customer.

item.title: The Handoff Is the Product
item.description: Air Canada, Klarna and Cursor learned the same lesson in public: the path from the bot to a human isn't the failure mode of an AI deployment. It's the feature that makes it safe to ship.

item.title: Prompt Injection Is a Permissions Bug
item.description: Assume the model will be tricked. The FDE's job is to decide, during scoping, what a tricked agent can reach — and to make sure it can't reach all three legs of the lethal trifecta at once.

item.title: Dry Run Before Autonomy
item.description: "Don't touch production" in a prompt is a request. A read-only credential is a control. Agent tool loops need dry runs, idempotency and scoped access before they need autonomy.

item.title: Rollback Is the Feature
item.description: The most instructive AI incidents of 2025 weren't fixed by better models. They were fixed by how fast someone could get back to the last known good state.

item.title: The Title Is The Tell
item.description: Fragmented FDE titles are not confusion — they are price discovery for deployment risk.

item.title: Not Yet Is the Deliverable
item.description: The best FDEs aren't measured by what they ship — they're measured by what they refuse to build until the data proves it's ready.

item.title: The Roadmap Is Not a Wish List
item.description: Internal advocacy is not lobbying. It is turning field pain into an eval product wants to ship.

item.title: What the Title Actually Prices
item.description: The title on your offer letter isn't describing the work — it's describing the pricing bracket.

item.title: The Title Isn't the Job
item.description: An 'FDE' title doesn't describe a role — it describes a company's bet about how software gets sold.

item.title: The Title Is the Price
item.description: Your title isn't describing your work. It's naming who absorbs the cost when an engagement goes sideways.

item.title: Same Work, Different Price
item.description: The title fragmentation in FDE-adjacent roles isn't a taxonomy — it's a pricing mechanism. Same responsibilities, 30% comp gap, anchored to five words.

item.title: Code Is Just a Receipt
item.description: In forward-deployed engineering, discovery isn't a prelude to the engagement. It IS the engagement. The code that follows is just the receipt.

item.title: The Code You Don't Write
item.description: The real product an FDE ships is a "don't build" list. Everything else is evidence for why each item belongs on it.

item.title: Lost Before You Type
item.description: Every failed engagement was lost in the first two weeks. The code just hadn't been written yet.

item.title: You're Not Deploying, You're Correcting
item.description: Your highest-output work isn't what you ship to the customer. It's what you ship back to your own product team.

item.title: Your Real Job Is Roadmap
item.description: The FDE's highest-leverage output isn't code deployed — it's field signal that changes the roadmap.

item.title: What the Job Selects For
item.description: The FDE role doesn't select for people skills. It selects for the ability to know the customer is wrong and say nothing — for three weeks.
